title: was ruled invalid by two European courts.
description:
was ruled invalid by two European courts. Apple patented sliding a finger across the screen to unlock the phone. Courts in Germany and the Netherlands later found that patent should never have been granted.

An Apple interface designer working on how to unlock the iPhone without a keypad. His team tried a two-finger slide and a twisting door-handle gesture, both rejected for needing two hands, before settling on one long horizontal swipe.

A small Swedish phone maker had already shipped the same idea. Neonode had already released a touchscreen phone with its own slide-to-unlock gesture. Germany's Federal Patent Court named that phone directly in 2013 when it threw out every one of Apple's claims, and rejected all 14 changes Apple proposed to save the patent.

like dragging a bolt across a door. That is the exact comparison Apple's own team used. The swipe ran horizontally rather than vertically, partly so the phone could be unlocked with one finger, and partly so it would not unlock itself while sitting in a pocket.

The gesture that made the crowd gasp in 2007 was ruled unpatentable by 2013, and gone from iPhones by 2016.

Sources:
- https://www.cultofmac.com/apple-history/slide-to-unlock-patent - read in full 7 Sep 2026: Cult of Mac (Luke Dormehl). Establishes that Apple filed a patent application for slide to unlock on 23 December 2005; that designer Bas Ording has described the team trying a two-finger slide, pressing two points at once, and a twisting door-handle gesture before settling on a single horizontal swipe, modelled on dragging a bolt across a door; that the gesture drew audible gasps at the 2007 iPhone unveiling; and that Apple retired it as the default lock screen with iOS 10 in 2016, after Touch ID arrived on the iPhone 5s in 2013 and before Face ID arrived in 2017.
- https://www.engadget.com/2013-04-05-german-court-finds-apples-slide-to-unlock-patent-invalid.html - read in full 7 Sep 2026: Engadget (Yoni Heisler, 5 April 2013). Establishes that Germany's Federal Patent Court invalidated every claim of Apple's European patent EP1964022 for slide to unlock, rejected all 14 amendments Apple proposed to save it, and that the ruling turned on a Swedish touchscreen phone, the Neonode N1m, which demonstrated its own slide-to-unlock gesture before Apple's patent application; also notes a Dutch court invalidated the same patent on the same grounds.
